title: How Solar Became the World's Cheapest Energy Source
paragraphs: We've known for nearly 200 years that light from the sun can be used to generate electricity, and the first solar cells were built as early as 1883.
However, the challenge has always been efficiency.

Those first solar cells could convert less than 1% of the sun's energy into electricity — a rate too low to be useful. In fact, the first practical solar cell wouldn't be made until 1954, at Bell Labs in New Jersey, with an efficiency of just 6%.
Thanks to advances in materials science and cell design, commercially available cells now typically achieve about 20% efficiency, while laboratory experiments have hit nearly 50%.

That rising efficiency has had real-world financial effects — with the International Energy Agency declaring in 2020 that, for certain projects, solar "is now the cheapest source of electricity in history."
That cost effectiveness has also come thanks to rising production efficiency — which ties back to decisions in Germany and China in the early 2000s.

Germany heavily incentivized rooftop solar panel installation at a time when China was rapidly expanding its solar cell manufacturing capacity. China further ramped up production to meet demand — and when that demand plummeted due to the global financial crisis at the end of the 2000s, China focused on developing its domestic market.
Production efficiencies only increased as research on next-generation cells continued — and China now gets 13% of its power from solar energy.
And China's cheap, efficient cells have opened up possibilities around the world.

For people in remote villages in countries with poor electrical infrastructure, it's much easier to install a rooftop solar panel than to wait for a power line to be connected to your home. And even for a small factory, it has become just as cost-effective to set up a solar system as it is to establish new coal or gas capacity.

Meanwhile, the sun isn't affected by politics, tariffs or trade blockades — offering many countries and communities a level of independence and economic stability along with electricity that only gets cheaper year by year.
